title: Does Chain-of-Thought Reliance Follow a Scaling Law?Larger Models Follow Their Steps More, Independent of Post-Training

paper.title: Does Chain-of-Thought Reliance Follow a Scaling Law? Larger Models Follow Their Steps More, Independent of Post-Training
paper.abstract:
Abstract Monitoring a model’s chain of thought (CoT) is useful for safety only if the
final answer actually depends on the written steps. Prior measurements of this
dependence use natural tasks on which the model’s true reasoning is unknown. We
measure it against an exact ground truth. On a synthetic box-swap task every
intermediate state is known, so we can replace one step inside a model’s own
chain with a wrong but valid state and check whether the continuation and the
answer follow the edit. We evaluate 25 open-weight models—Qwen3 (0.6B–14B,
base and post-trained), Gemma 3 (1B–12B), Llama 3 (1B–8B) and eight OLMo 2
pretraining checkpoints—on 7,200 items each, using a single 16 GB GPU. We
find five results. (1) Reliance rises with size and saturates. In Qwen3 the answer follows
an edited step 16–18% of the time at 0.6B and 97–100% at 14B; a saturating
logistic in log ⁡ N \log N fits with midpoint near 1B ( R 2 = 0.89 R^{2}=0.89 ), and Gemma 3 and
Llama 3 rise the same way. (2) Capability is the main driver. Across all 25 models, reliance and
step accuracy correlate at r = 0.99 r=0.99 ; equally capable models are about equally
reliant, whatever their size or family. (3) Size still matters at matched correctness. Counting only problems the
model solved correctly before the edit, reliance still increases with size among
capable models ( ρ = 0.80 \rho=0.80 , p = 0.002 p=0.002 ). (4) Post-training does not change reliance. Base and post-trained Qwen3
differ by at most 0.03 from 4B upward; the one large gap (1.7B) coincides with a
large capability gap. (5) No model up to 14B solves the task internally. Without written steps,
every capable model is at chance once a problem has four or more swaps.
OLMo 2 checkpoints never become capable on the task, so the training-token axis
is reported as a capability result and a limitation. On tasks that need
step-by-step computation, scale makes the chain of thought more load-bearing,
not less, which supports monitoring it in that regime.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Chain-of-thought prompting ( Wei et al., 2022b ) turns hidden computation into visible text, and reading that text has become a candidate safety tool ( Korbak et al., 2025 , Baker et al., 2025 ) . The tool only works if the written steps are load-bearing : if the model’s answer would be the same whatever the steps said, the chain is a narrative rather than a record. Measuring this property, often called CoT faithfulness, is hard on natural tasks because the model’s true reasoning is not observable. Existing evidence is mixed. Lanham et al. (2023) intervene on chains (truncation, inserted mistakes, paraphrase) and find that, on many tasks, larger models depend less on their chains; Bentham et al. (2024) show that this measure is strongly correlated with accuracy and that much of the apparent unfaithfulness of small models disappears once answer bias is controlled. Turpin et al. (2023) and Chen et al. (2025) show that stated reasoning can omit factors that demonstrably drive the answer. Emmons et al. (2025) argue that the picture changes when the chain is necessary for the task. These results leave open a basic scaling question: as models grow, do they rely on their written steps more or less, and is this governed by size, training data, or post-training? Answering it needs three things existing work lacks at once: (i) a ground truth for every intermediate step, so an edit’s effect is unambiguous; (ii) a task on which the chain is genuinely needed, so reliance is not trivially zero; and (iii) many models that vary one factor at a time. We provide all three with a deliberately simple design. Models track four lettered boxes through k k position swaps, writing the full state after each swap. Because every state is determined, we can (a) score each written step exactly, (b) measure accuracy with and without the chain, and (c) replace one step inside the model’s own chain with a wrong but valid state and let it continue. The follows-edit rate —how often the continuation and the answer are consistent with the corrupted state—is an exact, item-level measure of how much the answer depends on what was written.

sections.heading: Findings.
sections.text: (1) Reliance scales with size and saturates. In all three families with size series, the follows-edit rate rises monotonically with parameters; in Qwen3 it fits a saturating logistic in log ⁡ N \log N with midpoint near 1B and is at 0.97–1.00 by 14B (Figure 2 , Table 2 ). (2) Capability is the operative variable. Across all 25 models, reliance and step accuracy are almost perfectly correlated ( r = 0.99 r=0.99 ); at matched capability, a 1.7B Qwen3, a 4B Gemma 3 and an 8B Llama 3 are about equally reliant (Figure 3 ). This confirms, with an exact ground truth, the accuracy–faithfulness coupling reported by Bentham et al. (2024) . (3) Size matters beyond correctness. Restricting to problems the model solved correctly before the edit, reliance still increases with size among capable models ( ρ = 0.80 \rho=0.80 , p = 0.002 p=0.002 ). (4) Post-training is not the driver. Base and post-trained Qwen3 checkpoints are within ± 0.03 \pm 0.03 in reliance from 4B upward; the one large gap (1.7B) coincides with a large capability gap (Table 3 ). (5) No internal shortcut up to 14B. Without a chain, every capable model is at chance (mean 0.041 vs. 1 / 24 = 0.042 1/24=0.042 ) for k ≥ 4 k\geq 4 ; only two-swap problems show size-dependent internal solving (0.09 to 0.58 in Qwen3). The OLMo 2 pretraining checkpoints (1B and 7B, 0.3T–4T tokens) never reach the capability threshold, so the training-token axis is reported as a capability result and a limitation.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: (i) An exact, ground-truth protocol for measuring CoT reliance by in-chain step edits, runnable on a single 16 GB GPU; (ii) to our knowledge, the first scaling study of CoT reliance measured against an exact ground truth, with matched base and post-trained checkpoints at every size; (iii) evidence that, on tasks requiring serial computation, reliance follows capability and saturates rather than eroding with scale, reconciling this regime with prior inverse-scaling observations; and (iv) released items, generations and analysis code.

sections.heading: Measuring CoT faithfulness.
sections.text: Lanham et al. (2023) test whether answers change when chains are truncated, corrupted or paraphrased, and report that larger models are often less faithful, an inverse-scaling pattern. Bentham et al. (2024) replicate this setup across three model families and find that, after normalising for a model’s bias toward particular answer choices, small models look far less unfaithful and the normalised metric is strongly correlated with accuracy ( R 2 = 0.74 R^{2}=0.74 ), raising doubts about whether it measures faithfulness or capability. Our capability analysis (Section 4.3 ) addresses this concern directly, with an exact ground truth and a correct-prefix control. Turpin et al. (2023) show that biasing features can steer answers without being mentioned, and Chen et al. (2025) extend this to reasoning models; across twelve open-weight reasoning models, Young (2026) find that training method and model family predict hint acknowledgment more strongly than parameter count, and Hase and Potts (2026) find that larger models are not more faithful out of the box. These works measure whether a chain discloses an influencing cue, a different property from whether the answer depends on the written steps. Paul et al. (2024) measure and train for causal use of intermediate steps, Tutek et al. (2025) measure parametric faithfulness by unlearning reasoning steps, and Ye et al. (2026) corrupt individual steps and measure the drop in answer confidence, finding that late steps matter little. These works use natural or benchmark tasks where the correct intermediate reasoning is not uniquely defined, so an edit’s “correct” downstream effect must be inferred. Our task removes that ambiguity: every intermediate state and every consequence of an edit is computable.

sections.heading: Robustness to corrupted steps.
sections.text: Vaithinathan Aravindan and Kejriwal (2026) inject errors into mathematical chains for 13 models and find that larger models lose much less accuracy, i.e. they are more robust to corrupted steps. This is a different quantity from ours and, as we discuss in Section 5 , the two results are compatible.

sections.heading: Monitorability and necessity.
sections.text: Korbak et al. (2025) frame CoT monitoring as a valuable but fragile safety opportunity, and Baker et al. (2025) show that optimisation pressure on chains can produce obfuscation. Wang et al. (2026) find in MonitorBench that more capable models tend to be less monitorable, but that monitorability is higher when the decision-critical factors shape the intermediate reasoning rather than only the final answer. Emmons et al. (2025) argue that when a chain is necessary for a task, models struggle to evade monitors, and Pfau et al. (2024) show that some computation can be moved into filler tokens. Our results give a quantitative, scaling-level version of the necessity argument: on a task where the direct answer is at chance, reliance increases with scale.

sections.heading: Why CoT helps on serial tasks.
sections.text: Theory shows that chains extend what fixed-depth transformers can compute, especially for inherently serial problems ( Feng et al., 2023 , Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024 , Li et al., 2024 ) . Permutation and entity tracking is a canonical example; Kim and Schuster (2023) study box-content tracking in language models. We use this class of task precisely because direct computation should fail as k k grows, which we confirm empirically.

sections.heading: Scaling.
sections.text: Scaling laws describe loss as a function of parameters and data ( Kaplan et al., 2020 , Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) ; downstream abilities can appear abruptly ( Wei et al., 2022a ) , though apparent emergence can depend on the metric ( Schaeffer et al., 2023 ) . We report both a continuous reliance measure and its relation to capability, so that a jump in one can be checked against the other.

sections.heading: 3.1 Task
sections.text: A problem consists of an initial arrangement of letters A–D in boxes 1–4 and a list of k k swaps of box positions, k ∈ { 2 , 4 , 8 , 12 , 16 , 24 } k\in\{2,4,8,12,16,24\} . We generate 300 problems per k k (1,800 in total). The prompt contains an instruction and three worked examples ( k = 2 , 3 , 4 k=2,3,4 ) in the exact target format, in which every step restates its swap and the full state: Step 3 (swap 1 and 2): 1:A 2:B 3:C 4:D , followed by a final Answer: line. With four letters there are 4 ! = 24 4!=24 final states, so chance accuracy is 1 / 24 ≈ 0.042 1/24\approx 0.042 . Earlier pilots with five unlabelled boxes produced near-zero step accuracy for all small models; labelled positions and restated swaps were adopted so that the task measures state tracking rather than format following.

sections.heading: 3.2 Conditions
sections.text: Each problem is rendered in four conditions; three are analysed here. CoT : the model writes all steps and the answer. Direct : the model must output the answer line only. Edit : the prompt includes the start of a solution, steps 1 . . m 1..m ( 1 ≤ m < k 1\leq m<k ), in which the state at step m m is replaced by a different valid arrangement; the model continues from step m + 1 m+1 . A fourth control condition is generated for every problem but not analysed in this paper.

sections.heading: 3.3 Metrics
sections.text: A line-based parser reads each output up to the first answer line and discards malformed states (for example, a letter appearing twice). Compliance is the fraction of outputs with well-formed steps and an answer. Prefix accuracy , our capability measure, is the fraction of CoT runs whose states are correct up to the edit position. CoT and direct accuracy are final-answer accuracies. Each edited run is classified as follows-edit (the continuation and answer equal the result of applying the remaining swaps to the corrupted state), repair (it returns to the true trajectory), wrong-other , or invalid . The follows-edit rate is our reliance measure. Because a model that cannot track the state may fail to follow an edit for reasons unrelated to reliance, we also report it conditional on a correct prefix , i.e. on problems where the model’s own unedited chain was correct up to step m m .

sections.heading: 3.4 Models
sections.text: Qwen3 ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) : 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, 8B and 14B, each as a base and a post-trained checkpoint (10 models), trained on 36T tokens at every size; the post-trained models are run with thinking disabled. Gemma 3 ( Gemma Team, 2025 ) : 1B, 4B and 12B instruction-tuned. Llama 3 ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) : 3.2-1B, 3.2-3B and 3.1-8B instruction-tuned. OLMo 2 ( Team OLMo et al., 2024 ) : 1B checkpoints at 336B, 944B, 1972B and 2978B tokens plus the final release, and 7B checkpoints at 1934B and 2924B tokens plus the final release. OLMo 2 is the only family that releases intermediate checkpoints of the same model, which is what a training-token axis requires: in Gemma 3 and Llama 3 token count rises together with size, and in Qwen3 it does not vary. Size N N is the non-embedding parameter count. A 4-bit NF4 ( Dettmers et al., 2023 ) copy of Qwen3-4B serves as a quantization ablation.

sections.heading: 3.5 Inference and statistics
sections.text: All runs are inference-only on one NVIDIA T4 (16 GB). Models that do not fit in 16 GB at 16-bit precision are loaded with NF4 weights. Generation is greedy and stops at the first answer line, which does not affect scoring because the parser ignores text after it. A checkpointed runner survives preemption, and every model in the paper has all 7,200 generations. Confidence intervals use 1,000 bootstrap resamples over problems. sections.heading: 4.1 The task requires the chain
sections.text: Figure 1 shows final-answer accuracy by k k . With a chain, capable models stay far above chance up to k = 24 k=24 (Qwen3-14B: 1.00 at every k k ). Without one, every model is near chance from k = 4 k=4 : across the 12 capable models in the three families, direct accuracy for k ≥ 4 k\geq 4 ranges from 0.002 to 0.052 with mean 0.041 (chance 0.042), and for the largest models it is not significantly above chance (binomial p = 0.61 p=0.61 for Qwen3-14B, p = 0.11 p=0.11 for Gemma 3-12B). Only at k = 2 k=2 does direct accuracy grow with size (Qwen3 post-trained 0.09 to 0.58; Spearman ρ = 0.82 \rho=0.82 with N N over the three families). The models therefore start to compute two swaps internally, but none of them, up to 14B, can do four without writing the steps. Figure 1: Final-answer accuracy with (CoT) and without (Direct) the written chain, by number of swaps k k , for the post-trained models. The dotted line is chance ( 1 / 24 1/24 ). Direct accuracy is at chance for k ≥ 4 k\geq 4 at every size.

sections.heading: 4.2 Reliance rises with size and saturates
sections.text: Table 1 and Figure 2 report the follows-edit rate. In Qwen3 it rises from 0.16 (base) and 0.18 (post-trained) at 0.6B to 0.97 and 1.00 at 14B. A saturating logistic in log ⁡ N \log N fits the ten Qwen3 models with R 2 = 0.89 R^{2}=0.89 and a midpoint of 1.07B; the fitted floor is 0.00 (Table 2 ). The same monotone increase appears in Gemma 3 (0.27, 0.85, 0.98 at 1B, 4B, 12B) and Llama 3 (0.07, 0.29, 0.73 at 1B, 3B, 8B). Pooling the three families, Spearman ρ = 0.90 \rho=0.90 ; the pooled logistic fit is weaker ( R 2 = 0.74 R^{2}=0.74 ) because families reach the same reliance at different sizes. Edited models rarely repair the corruption: repair is at most 0.06 for any model (Table 6 ), and answers that contradict the model’s own final step are at most 0.02. When capable models do not follow an edit, they mostly produce a different wrong trajectory, not the correct answer. Figure 2: Follows-edit rate vs. non-embedding parameters, with 95% bootstrap CIs. Filled markers: post-trained; open markers: base. Dotted curve: saturating logistic fit to the ten Qwen3 models.

sections.heading: 4.3 Capability is the operative variable
sections.text: Figure 3 plots reliance against prefix accuracy for all 25 models. The points collapse onto one curve (Pearson r = 0.99 r=0.99 , Spearman ρ = 0.98 \rho=0.98 ), including the OLMo 2 checkpoints, which sit at the low end. Models of different sizes and families with similar capability have similar reliance: Qwen3-1.7B (prefix 0.93, reliance 0.85), Gemma 3-4B (0.94, 0.85) and Llama 3.1-8B (0.85, 0.73). Size matters for reliance mainly through capability; families differ in how many parameters they need to reach a given capability. This confirms and sharpens the observation of Bentham et al. (2024) that a dependence-based faithfulness measure tracks accuracy ( R 2 = 0.74 R^{2}=0.74 in their setting): with an exact ground truth for every step, the coupling is near-perfect. A tight coupling could arise mechanically, since a model that cannot track the state cannot propagate an edit either. The conditional measure addresses this. Restricting to problems on which the model’s own prefix was correct, reliance is higher for small models (Qwen3-0.6B: 0.44 vs. 0.18 unconditional) but still increases with size: among the 12 capable models, Spearman ρ = 0.80 \rho=0.80 ( p = 0.002 p=0.002 ), and in Qwen3 the conditional curve fits a logistic with R 2 = 0.91 R^{2}=0.91 . Even when a small model gets the steps right, its answer depends on them less than a large model’s does. Reliance is therefore not merely accuracy in disguise: the size trend survives once correctness is held fixed. Figure 3: Follows-edit rate vs. prefix accuracy for all 25 models. Reliance and capability are almost perfectly correlated across families and training stages.

sections.heading: 4.4 Post-training does not change reliance
sections.text: Table 3 and Figure 4 compare base and post-trained Qwen3 at each size, conditional on a correct prefix. From 4B upward the two are within 0.03 ( − 0.022 -0.022 , + 0.008 +0.008 , + 0.022 +0.022 ). The one large difference, + 0.278 +0.278 at 1.7B, coincides with a large capability difference (prefix accuracy 0.533 vs. 0.934), consistent with Section 4.3 . On this task, post-training raises reliance only by raising capability where the base model is still weak. Figure 4: Qwen3 base vs. post-trained follows-edit rate, restricted to problems on which the model’s own unedited prefix was correct.

sections.heading: 4.5 Quantization
sections.text: Loading Qwen3-4B in NF4 lowers prefix accuracy from 0.962 to 0.883 and reliance from 0.913 to 0.869 (Table 1 ). Because the largest models are quantized, any bias from quantization works against the size trend, so the reported increase is, if anything, conservative.

sections.heading: 4.6 Training tokens: a capability floor
sections.text: Table 4 and Figure 5 report the OLMo 2 checkpoints. All five 1B checkpoints are at the floor (prefix accuracy ≤ 0.014 \leq 0.014 ) across a 12-fold increase in training tokens. At 7B, the 1.9T and 2.9T checkpoints are also at the floor (0.028, 0.032), and only the released checkpoint rises, to 0.198, with direct accuracy at k = 2 k=2 rising to 0.217. That checkpoint differs from the 2.9T one not only in tokens but also in OLMo 2’s math-heavy mid-training stage ( Team OLMo et al., 2024 ) , so we cannot attribute the jump to token count. No checkpoint reaches the capability threshold, so the token axis cannot support a reliance scaling curve. The one checkpoint with enough conditional data ( olmo2-7b-main , n = 356 n=356 ) has conditional reliance 0.303, within the range of similarly capable models from other families (0.14–0.49 for prefix accuracy 0.15–0.40), consistent with the capability account. Figure 5: OLMo 2 prefix accuracy and follows-edit rate across pretraining checkpoints. The final release includes mid-training. No checkpoint crosses the 0.5 capability threshold (dashed).

sections.heading: Reconciling with inverse scaling.
sections.text: Lanham et al. (2023) found that larger models often depend less on their chains, and Wang et al. (2026) find that more capable models tend to be less monitorable. Our results do not contradict this; they locate a regime where the opposite holds. When a task is within a model’s internal capacity, the chain can be redundant and larger models may answer correctly whatever it says. When the task needs more serial steps than the model can do internally—here, every k ≥ 4 k\geq 4 problem for every model up to 14B—the chain is the computation, and larger models use it more consistently. This matches MonitorBench’s own observation that monitorability is higher when decision-critical factors shape the intermediate reasoning. The k = 2 k=2 result marks the boundary: as direct accuracy rises with size there, we would expect reliance on short chains to eventually fall. The scaling of reliance should therefore be stated relative to the task’s difficulty for the model, which supports the necessity argument of Emmons et al. (2025) .

sections.heading: Reconciling with robustness to corrupted steps.
sections.text: Vaithinathan Aravindan and Kejriwal (2026) report that larger models are more robust to errors injected into mathematical chains, which might seem to contradict our finding that larger models follow edits more often. The two settings differ in what a correct continuation looks like. An arithmetic error in a math chain usually contradicts information that is still present in the problem, so a capable model can recompute the affected quantity and recover; robustness there reflects re-derivation from the question. Our edit replaces the entire state with a different valid arrangement, so the only way to “recover” is to silently re-derive every preceding swap from the start while ignoring the written state. Following the edit is the behaviour that reflects genuine reliance on the chain, and it is what larger models do. Robustness to local errors and reliance on the written state are therefore distinct properties, and both can rise with scale.

sections.heading: Implications for monitoring.
sections.text: For tasks that genuinely need multi-step computation, the evidence here favours CoT monitoring: up to 14B, the more capable the model, the more its answer is determined by what it wrote, and edits are almost never silently repaired. The caveat is the open end of the curve. Our largest models saturate on our metric, so the data cannot show whether reliance would eventually fall once models can do long chains internally. The direct-accuracy curve at small k k is the variable to watch.

sections.heading: What a “scaling law” means here.
sections.text: Reliance is well described by a saturating function of log ⁡ N \log N within a family, but the more fundamental regularity is its relation to capability, which holds across families, sizes and training stages. A useful predictive form is therefore two-stage: scale predicts capability on the task, and capability predicts reliance.

sections.heading: 6 Limitations
sections.text: One task family. Box-swap tracking is a clean, controllable serial task; reliance on natural-language, mathematical or agentic reasoning may scale differently. Size range and saturation. Models go up to 14B, and the largest saturate near 1.0, which limits what the top of the curve can show. Token axis. OLMo 2 checkpoints up to 7B never reach the capability threshold, so we cannot estimate how reliance scales with training tokens; the 13B OLMo 2 checkpoints were not run within our compute budget. Family confounds. Across families, data, architecture and recipe differ together; we therefore draw size conclusions within families and use pooling only as corroboration. Behavioural measure. Following an edit shows that the answer depends on the written state; it does not show that no parallel internal computation occurs. Single edit type and greedy decoding. We edit one step to one wrong valid state and decode greedily; other edit types or sampling may give different rates. Quantization. Large models run in NF4; the 4B ablation suggests a small downward effect. Reasoning modes. Qwen3’s thinking mode was disabled; models trained to reason in long hidden traces were not studied.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We measured how much a model’s answer depends on its own chain of thought, using exact in-chain step edits on a task with known intermediate states, across 25 open models from four families on a single 16 GB GPU. The results support five conclusions. 1. Reliance on the chain rises with model size and saturates. The follows-edit rate climbs from 0.16–0.18 at Qwen3-0.6B to 0.97–1.00 at Qwen3-14B, fits a saturating logistic in log ⁡ N \log N with midpoint near 1B ( R 2 = 0.89 R^{2}=0.89 ), and rises monotonically in Gemma 3 (0.27, 0.85, 0.98) and Llama 3 (0.07, 0.29, 0.73) as well. 2. Capability, not size itself, is the main driver. Across all 25 models, reliance and step accuracy correlate at r = 0.99 r=0.99 . Families need different numbers of parameters to reach a given capability, but at matched capability their reliance is similar. 3. Size still matters once correctness is controlled. On problems the model solved correctly before the edit, reliance still increases with size among capable models ( ρ = 0.80 \rho=0.80 , p = 0.002 p=0.002 ), so the trend is not only an artefact of small models failing the task. 4. Post-training does not change reliance. Base and post-trained Qwen3 differ by at most 0.03 from 4B upward; the only large gap, at 1.7B, matches a large capability gap (prefix accuracy 0.53 vs. 0.93). 5. No model up to 14B solves the task without its chain. Direct accuracy is at chance (0.041 vs. 0.042) for every capable model once a problem has four or more swaps; internal solving appears only for two-swap problems (0.09 to 0.58 in Qwen3). The OLMo 2 checkpoints never reached the capability threshold at 1B or 7B, so the effect of training tokens on reliance remains open; they nevertheless fall on the same reliance–capability curve as the other families. Taken together, on tasks that need step-by-step computation, scaling makes the chain of thought more load-bearing, not less. This supports chain-of-thought monitoring in that regime and identifies direct-answer accuracy as the signal to watch: if larger models begin to solve multi-step problems without writing the steps, reliance on the chain may start to fall.

Larger Models Follow Their Steps More, Independent of Post-Training Esther Xin Affiliation: Independent Researcher Email: estherxin0011@gmail.com Affiliation: Code and data: https://github.com/ethxin0011/cot-scale-reliance Abstract Monitoring a model’s chain of thought (CoT) is useful for safety only if the final answer actually depends on the written steps. Prior measurements of this dependence use natural tasks on which the model’s true reasoning is unknown. We measure it against an exact ground truth. On a synthetic box-swap task every intermediate state is known, so we can replace one step inside a model’s own chain with a wrong but valid state and check whether the continuation and the answer follow the edit. We evaluate 25 open-weight models—Qwen3 (0.6B–14B, base and post-trained), Gemma 3 (1B–12B), Llama 3 (1B–8B) and eight OLMo 2 pretraining checkpoints—on 7,200 items each, using a single 16 GB GPU. We find five results. (1) Reliance rises with size and saturates. In Qwen3 the answer follows an edited step 16–18% of the time at 0.6B and 97–100% at 14B; a saturating logistic in log ⁡ N \log N fits with midpoint near 1B ( R 2 = 0.89 R^{2}=0.89 ), and Gemma 3 and Llama 3 rise the same way. (2) Capability is the main driver. Across all 25 models, reliance and step accuracy correlate at r = 0.99 r=0.99 ; equally capable models are about equally reliant, whatever their size or family. (3) Size still matters at matched correctness. Counting only problems the model solved correctly before the edit, reliance still increases with size among capable models ( ρ = 0.80 \rho=0.80 , p = 0.002 p=0.002 ). (4) Post-training does not change reliance. Base and post-trained Qwen3 differ by at most 0.03 from 4B upward; the one large gap (1.7B) coincides with a large capability gap. (5) No model up to 14B solves the task internally. Without written steps, every capable model is at chance once a problem has four or more swaps. OLMo 2 checkpoints never become capable on the task, so the training-token axis is reported as a capability result and a limitation. On tasks that need step-by-step computation, scale makes the chain of thought more load-bearing, not less, which supports monitoring it in that regime. 1 Introduction Chain-of-thought prompting ( Wei et al., 2022b ) turns hidden computation into visible text, and reading that text has become a candidate safety tool ( Korbak et al., 2025 , Baker et al., 2025 ) . The tool only works if the written steps are load-bearing : if the model’s answer would be the same whatever the steps said, the chain is a narrative rather than a record. Measuring this property, often called CoT faithfulness, is hard on natural tasks because the model’s true reasoning is not observable. Existing evidence is mixed. Lanham et al. (2023) intervene on chains (truncation, inserted mistakes, paraphrase) and find that, on many tasks, larger models depend less on their chains; Bentham et al. (2024) show that this measure is strongly correlated with accuracy and that much of the apparent unfaithfulness of small models disappears once answer bias is controlled. Turpin et al. (2023) and Chen et al. (2025) show that stated reasoning can omit factors that demonstrably drive the answer. Emmons et al. (2025) argue that the picture changes when the chain is necessary for the task. These results leave open a basic scaling question: as models grow, do they rely on their written steps more or less, and is this governed by size, training data, or post-training? Answering it needs three things existing work lacks at once: (i) a ground truth for every intermediate step, so an edit’s effect is unambiguous; (ii) a task on which the chain is genuinely needed, so reliance is not trivially zero; and (iii) many models that vary one factor at a time. We provide all three with a deliberately simple design. Models track four lettered boxes through k k position swaps, writing the full state after each swap. Because every state is determined, we can (a) score each written step exactly, (b) measure accuracy with and without the chain, and (c) replace one step inside the model’s own chain with a wrong but valid state and let it continue. The follows-edit rate —how often the continuation and the answer are consistent with the corrupted state—is an exact, item-level measure of how much the answer depends on what was written. Findings. (1) Reliance scales with size and saturates. In all three families with size series, the follows-edit rate rises monotonically with parameters; in Qwen3 it fits a saturating logistic in log ⁡ N \log N with midpoint near 1B and is at 0.97–1.00 by 14B (Figure 2 , Table 2 ). (2) Capability is the operative variable. Across all 25 models, reliance and step accuracy are almost perfectly correlated ( r = 0.99 r=0.99 ); at matched capability, a 1.7B Qwen3, a 4B Gemma 3 and an 8B Llama 3 are about equally reliant (Figure 3 ). This confirms, with an exact ground truth, the accuracy–faithfulness coupling reported by Bentham et al. (2024) . (3) Size matters beyond correctness. Restricting to problems the model solved correctly before the edit, reliance still increases with size among capable models ( ρ = 0.80 \rho=0.80 , p = 0.002 p=0.002 ). (4) Post-training is not the driver. Base and post-trained Qwen3 checkpoints are within ± 0.03 \pm 0.03 in reliance from 4B upward; the one large gap (1.7B) coincides with a large capability gap (Table 3 ). (5) No internal shortcut up to 14B. Without a chain, every capable model is at chance (mean 0.041 vs. 1 / 24 = 0.042 1/24=0.042 ) for k ≥ 4 k\geq 4 ; only two-swap problems show size-dependent internal solving (0.09 to 0.58 in Qwen3). The OLMo 2 pretraining checkpoints (1B and 7B, 0.3T–4T tokens) never reach the capability threshold, so the training-token axis is reported as a capability result and a limitation. Contributions. (i) An exact, ground-truth protocol for measuring CoT reliance by in-chain step edits, runnable on a single 16 GB GPU; (ii) to our knowledge, the first scaling study of CoT reliance measured against an exact ground truth, with matched base and post-trained checkpoints at every size; (iii) evidence that, on tasks requiring serial computation, reliance follows capability and saturates rather than eroding with scale, reconciling this regime with prior inverse-scaling observations; and (iv) released items, generations and analysis code. 2 Related Work Measuring CoT faithfulness. Lanham et al. (2023) test whether answers change when chains are truncated, corrupted or paraphrased, and report that larger models are often less faithful, an inverse-scaling pattern. Bentham et al. (2024) replicate this setup across three model families and find that, after normalising for a model’s bias toward particular answer choices, small models look far less unfaithful and the normalised metric is strongly correlated with accuracy ( R 2 = 0.74 R^{2}=0.74 ), raising doubts about whether it measures faithfulness or capability. Our capability analysis (Section 4.3 ) addresses this concern directly, with an exact ground truth and a correct-prefix control. Turpin et al. (2023) show that biasing features can steer answers without being mentioned, and Chen et al. (2025) extend this to reasoning models; across twelve open-weight reasoning models, Young (2026) find that training method and model family predict hint acknowledgment more strongly than parameter count, and Hase and Potts (2026) find that larger models are not more faithful out of the box. These works measure whether a chain discloses an influencing cue, a different property from whether the answer depends on the written steps. Paul et al. (2024) measure and train for causal use of intermediate steps, Tutek et al. (2025) measure parametric faithfulness by unlearning reasoning steps, and Ye et al. (2026) corrupt individual steps and measure the drop in answer confidence, finding that late steps matter little. These works use natural or benchmark tasks where the correct intermediate reasoning is not uniquely defined, so an edit’s “correct” downstream effect must be inferred. Our task removes that ambiguity: every intermediate state and every consequence of an edit is computable. Robustness to corrupted steps. Vaithinathan Aravindan and Kejriwal (2026) inject errors into mathematical chains for 13 models and find that larger models lose much less accuracy, i.e. they are more robust to corrupted steps. This is a different quantity from ours and, as we discuss in Section 5 , the two results are compatible. Monitorability and necessity. Korbak et al. (2025) frame CoT monitoring as a valuable but fragile safety opportunity, and Baker et al. (2025) show that optimisation pressure on chains can produce obfuscation. Wang et al. (2026) find in MonitorBench that more capable models tend to be less monitorable, but that monitorability is higher when the decision-critical factors shape the intermediate reasoning rather than only the final answer. Emmons et al. (2025) argue that when a chain is necessary for a task, models struggle to evade monitors, and Pfau et al. (2024) show that some computation can be moved into filler tokens. Our results give a quantitative, scaling-level version of the necessity argument: on a task where the direct answer is at chance, reliance increases with scale. Why CoT helps on serial tasks. Theory shows that chains extend what fixed-depth transformers can compute, especially for inherently serial problems ( Feng et al., 2023 , Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024 , Li et al., 2024 ) . Permutation and entity tracking is a canonical example; Kim and Schuster (2023) study box-content tracking in language models. We use this class of task precisely because direct computation should fail as k k grows, which we confirm empirically. Scaling. Scaling laws describe loss as a function of parameters and data ( Kaplan et al., 2020 , Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) ; downstream abilities can appear abruptly ( Wei et al., 2022a ) , though apparent emergence can depend on the metric ( Schaeffer et al., 2023 ) . We report both a continuous reliance measure and its relation to capability, so that a jump in one can be checked against the other. 3 Method 3.1 Task A problem consists of an initial arrangement of letters A–D in boxes 1–4 and a list of k k swaps of box positions, k ∈ { 2 , 4 , 8 , 12 , 16 , 24 } k\in\{2,4,8,12,16,24\} . We generate 300 problems per k k (1,800 in total). The prompt contains an instruction and three worked examples ( k = 2 , 3 , 4 k=2,3,4 ) in the exact target format, in which every step restates its swap and the full state: Step 3 (swap 1 and 2): 1:A 2:B 3:C 4:D , followed by a final Answer: line. With four letters there are 4 ! = 24 4!=24 final states, so chance accuracy is 1 / 24 ≈ 0.042 1/24\approx 0.042 . Earlier pilots with five unlabelled boxes produced near-zero step accuracy for all small models; labelled positions and restated swaps were adopted so that the task measures state tracking rather than format following. 3.2 Conditions Each problem is rendered in four conditions; three are analysed here. CoT : the model writes all steps and the answer. Direct : the model must output the answer line only. Edit : the prompt includes the start of a solution, steps 1 . . m 1..m ( 1 ≤ m < k 1\leq m<k ), in which the state at step m m is replaced by a different valid arrangement; the model continues from step m + 1 m+1 . A fourth control condition is generated for every problem but not analysed in this paper. 3.3 Metrics A line-based parser reads each output up to the first answer line and discards malformed states (for example, a letter appearing twice). Compliance is the fraction of outputs with well-formed steps and an answer. Prefix accuracy , our capability measure, is the fraction of CoT runs whose states are correct up to the edit position. CoT and direct accuracy are final-answer accuracies. Each edited run is classified as follows-edit (the continuation and answer equal the result of applying the remaining swaps to the corrupted state), repair (it returns to the true trajectory), wrong-other , or invalid . The follows-edit rate is our reliance measure. Because a model that cannot track the state may fail to follow an edit for reasons unrelated to reliance, we also report it conditional on a correct prefix , i.e. on problems where the model’s own unedited chain was correct up to step m m . 3.4 Models Qwen3 ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) : 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, 8B and 14B, each as a base and a post-trained checkpoint (10 models), trained on 36T tokens at every size; the post-trained models are run with thinking disabled. Gemma 3 ( Gemma Team, 2025 ) : 1B, 4B and 12B instruction-tuned. Llama 3 ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) : 3.2-1B, 3.2-3B and 3.1-8B instruction-tuned. OLMo 2 ( Team OLMo et al., 2024 ) : 1B checkpoints at 336B, 944B, 1972B and 2978B tokens plus the final release, and 7B checkpoints at 1934B and 2924B tokens plus the final release. OLMo 2 is the only family that releases intermediate checkpoints of the same model, which is what a training-token axis requires: in Gemma 3 and Llama 3 token count rises together with size, and in Qwen3 it does not vary. Size N N is the non-embedding parameter count. A 4-bit NF4 ( Dettmers et al., 2023 ) copy of Qwen3-4B serves as a quantization ablation. 3.5 Inference and statistics All runs are inference-only on one NVIDIA T4 (16 GB). Models that do not fit in 16 GB at 16-bit precision are loaded with NF4 weights. Generation is greedy and stops at the first answer line, which does not affect scoring because the parser ignores text after it. A checkpointed runner survives preemption, and every model in the paper has all 7,200 generations. Confidence intervals use 1,000 bootstrap resamples over problems. No checkpoint crosses the 0.5 capability threshold (dashed). 5 Discussion Reconciling with inverse scaling. Lanham et al. (2023) found that larger models often depend less on their chains, and Wang et al. (2026) find that more capable models tend to be less monitorable. Our results do not contradict this; they locate a regime where the opposite holds. When a task is within a model’s internal capacity, the chain can be redundant and larger models may answer correctly whatever it says. When the task needs more serial steps than the model can do internally—here, every k ≥ 4 k\geq 4 problem for every model up to 14B—the chain is the computation, and larger models use it more consistently. This matches MonitorBench’s own observation that monitorability is higher when decision-critical factors shape the intermediate reasoning. The k = 2 k=2 result marks the boundary: as direct accuracy rises with size there, we would expect reliance on short chains to eventually fall. The scaling of reliance should therefore be stated relative to the task’s difficulty for the model, which supports the necessity argument of Emmons et al. (2025) . Reconciling with robustness to corrupted steps. Vaithinathan Aravindan and Kejriwal (2026) report that larger models are more robust to errors injected into mathematical chains, which might seem to contradict our finding that larger models follow edits more often. The two settings differ in what a correct continuation looks like. An arithmetic error in a math chain usually contradicts information that is still present in the problem, so a capable model can recompute the affected quantity and recover; robustness there reflects re-derivation from the question. Our edit replaces the entire state with a different valid arrangement, so the only way to “recover” is to silently re-derive every preceding swap from the start while ignoring the written state. Following the edit is the behaviour that reflects genuine reliance on the chain, and it is what larger models do. Robustness to local errors and reliance on the written state are therefore distinct properties, and both can rise with scale. Implications for monitoring. For tasks that genuinely need multi-step computation, the evidence here favours CoT monitoring: up to 14B, the more capable the model, the more its answer is determined by what it wrote, and edits are almost never silently repaired. The caveat is the open end of the curve. Our largest models saturate on our metric, so the data cannot show whether reliance would eventually fall once models can do long chains internally. The direct-accuracy curve at small k k is the variable to watch. What a “scaling law” means here. Reliance is well described by a saturating function of log ⁡ N \log N within a family, but the more fundamental regularity is its relation to capability, which holds across families, sizes and training stages. A useful predictive form is therefore two-stage: scale predicts capability on the task, and capability predicts reliance. 6 Limitations One task family. Box-swap tracking is a clean, controllable serial task; reliance on natural-language, mathematical or agentic reasoning may scale differently. Size range and saturation. Models go up to 14B, and the largest saturate near 1.0, which limits what the top of the curve can show. Token axis. OLMo 2 checkpoints up to 7B never reach the capability threshold, so we cannot estimate how reliance scales with training tokens; the 13B OLMo 2 checkpoints were not run within our compute budget. Family confounds. Across families, data, architecture and recipe differ together; we therefore draw size conclusions within families and use pooling only as corroboration. Behavioural measure. Following an edit shows that the answer depends on the written state; it does not show that no parallel internal computation occurs. Single edit type and greedy decoding. We edit one step to one wrong valid state and decode greedily; other edit types or sampling may give different rates. Quantization. Large models run in NF4; the 4B ablation suggests a small downward effect. Reasoning modes. Qwen3’s thinking mode was disabled; models trained to reason in long hidden traces were not studied. 7 Conclusion We measured how much a model’s answer depends on its own chain of thought, using exact in-chain step edits on a task with known intermediate states, across 25 open models from four families on a single 16 GB GPU. The results support five conclusions. 1. Reliance on the chain rises with model size and saturates. The follows-edit rate climbs from 0.16–0.18 at Qwen3-0.6B to 0.97–1.00 at Qwen3-14B, fits a saturating logistic in log ⁡ N \log N with midpoint near 1B ( R 2 = 0.89 R^{2}=0.89 ), and rises monotonically in Gemma 3 (0.27, 0.85, 0.98) and Llama 3 (0.07, 0.29, 0.73) as well. 2. Capability, not size itself, is the main driver. Across all 25 models, reliance and step accuracy correlate at r = 0.99 r=0.99 . Families need different numbers of parameters to reach a given capability, but at matched capability their reliance is similar. 3. Size still matters once correctness is controlled. On problems the model solved correctly before the edit, reliance still increases with size among capable models ( ρ = 0.80 \rho=0.80 , p = 0.002 p=0.002 ), so the trend is not only an artefact of small models failing the task. 4. Post-training does not change reliance. Base and post-trained Qwen3 differ by at most 0.03 from 4B upward; the only large gap, at 1.7B, matches a large capability gap (prefix accuracy 0.53 vs. 0.93). 5. No model up to 14B solves the task without its chain. Direct accuracy is at chance (0.041 vs. 0.042) for every capable model once a problem has four or more swaps; internal solving appears only for two-swap problems (0.09 to 0.58 in Qwen3). The OLMo 2 checkpoints never reached the capability threshold at 1B or 7B, so the effect of training tokens on reliance remains open; they nevertheless fall on the same reliance–capability curve as the other families. Taken together, on tasks that need step-by-step computation, scaling makes the chain of thought more load-bearing, not less. This supports chain-of-thought monitoring in that regime and identifies direct-answer accuracy as the signal to watch: if larger models begin to solve multi-step problems without writing the steps, reliance on the chain may start to fall.
